qs.q: A 27‑year‑old woman with a history of deep‑vein thrombosis (treated 2 years ago) wants a hormonal method. Which option is classified as WHO MEC category 4 for her?
qs.e: Current or high‑risk VTE places combined hormonal contraception in category 4, so it must not be used. Progestogen‑only and non‑hormonal methods are acceptable.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of recurrent miscarriages and deep vein thrombosis presents with a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). Mixing studies fail to correct the aPTT. Which autoantibody subtype is typically responsible?
o: Anti-factor VIII inhibitory alloantibodies neutralizing coagulation cascades
Antiphospholipid antibodies interfering with phospholipid-dependent tests
Anti-platelet factor 4 antibodies inducing massive cellular aggregation
Anti-thrombin III neutralizing antibodies blocking endogenous anticoagulation
Anti-von Willebrand factor antibodies accelerating multimer clearance
qs.e: Antiphospholipid antibodies paradoxically prolong in vitro phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays while causing in vivo thrombosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with deep vein thrombosis and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis associated with a newly diagnosed pancreatic malignancy. What is the classic eponym for this finding?
qs.e: Migratory thrombophlebitis and deep vein thrombosis associated with visceral malignancies such as pancreatic cancer is known as Trousseau's sign. Courvoisier's law relates to a palpable non-tender gallbladder in painless jaundice.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis presents with leg swelling and varicose veins. Which underlying mechanism is most likely responsible for her condition?
o: Congenital weakness of the vein wall
qs.e: Secondary varicose veins are caused by post-DVT obstruction, whereas primary varicose veins result from valve incompetence or wall weakness. The history of DVT points to a secondary etiology.
qs.s: Varicose Veins and Chronic Venous Insufficiency of the Leg: MCQs

qs.q: A 53‑year‑old woman is recovering after endovascular coiling of a ruptured aneurysm. When is it safest to start low‑dose heparin for deep‑vein thrombosis prophylaxis?
o: Once the aneurysm has been secured
Immediately on admission, prior to the coiling procedure
qs.e: Heparin is initiated only after the aneurysm is definitively secured to avoid increasing the risk of rebleeding. Mechanical methods are used earlier, and the other timings risk hemorrhagic complications.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops deep vein thrombosis and recurrent miscarriages. Laboratory testing reveals antibodies that prolong in vitro coagulation assays. What is the paradoxical in vivo effect of these antibodies?
o: They directly inhibit platelet production within the bone marrow
They induce rapid lysis of circulating red blood cells via complement
They cause severe life-threatening spontaneous bleeding episodes
They exert a procoagulant effect causing recurrent vascular thrombosis
qs.e: Antiphospholipid antibodies or lupus anticoagulants prolong in vitro coagulation assays but actually exert a procoagulant effect in vivo, causing vascular thrombosis. They do not cause spontaneous bleeding disorders or direct red blood cell lysis.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man presents with painful lower extremity swelling after a long international flight. Which complication specifically distinguishes deep vein thrombosis from superficial varicose veins?
o: Major risk of fatal pulmonary embolism
Local skin ulceration over the medial malleolus
qs.e: Deep vein thrombosis carries a high risk of life-threatening pulmonary embolism due to the large caliber of the vessels. In contrast, superficial varicose veins rarely cause pulmonary embolism because thrombi remain localized.

qs.q: Which of the following is a classic component of Virchow's Triad governing the pathogenesis of deep vein thrombosis?
qs.e: Virchow's Triad comprises stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, which together promote deep vein thrombosis. The other terms describe vascular ectasias, pressure changes, or specific syndromes rather than the triad components.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with HIV presents with unilateral calf swelling; what is your immediate management and why? — Assess risk, obtain D‑dimer, start LMWH if high risk; HIV increases hypercoagulability.
How does the Wells score influence your diagnostic pathway in a setting without ultrasound? — High score → treat empirically; low score → D‑dimer to rule out.
What features distinguish cellulitis from DVT on bedside exam? — Cellulitis shows diffuse erythema, fever, and no calf circumference difference; DVT has localized swelling, pain on calf compression.
Why is unfractionated heparin preferred if the patient may need urgent surgery? — It can be rapidly reversed with protamine, unlike LMWH.
Explain why a normal D‑dimer does not completely exclude proximal DVT in a patient with active TB. — TB raises baseline D‑dimer; clinical judgment remains essential.
What complications should you monitor for after starting anticoagulation in a patient with sickle cell disease? — Bleeding, heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia, and recurrent vaso‑occlusive crises.
When is an inferior vena cava filter indicated in low‑resource hospitals? — When anticoagulation is contraindicated and there is high risk of PE.
How would you counsel a patient about compression stockings after DVT? — Wear graduated stockings for at least 6 months to reduce post‑thrombotic syndrome; ensure proper fit.
ai.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is clot formation in deep veins, usually of the lower limbs. Recognise risk factors, clinical clues, and limited investigations in low‑resource settings to start timely anticoagulation and prevent fatal pulmonary embolism.

b: Incidence rises with age, pregnancy, HIV, TB, malaria, sickle cell disease.
sections.p: DVT is a thrombus in a deep vein, most often the femoral or popliteal veins. It can be provoked (immobility, surgery, infection) or unprovoked. In low‑resource hospitals, presentation may be delayed and diagnostic tools limited.

b: Provoking factors: recent surgery, long travel, immobilisation, infection (e.g., TB, malaria).
Hypercoagulable states common in Africa: HIV, sickle cell, schistosomiasis.
sections.p: Virchow's triad—stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability—drives clot formation. Assess severity with the Wells clinical prediction score (if possible) and consider proximal vs distal clot location.

b: Homan's sign (pain on dorsiflexion) is unreliable but may be present.
Look for risk factors and consider bedside ultrasound if available.
sections.p: Patients present with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and sometimes a visible cord. Absence of classic signs does not exclude DVT, especially in the obese or those with peripheral neuropathy.

t.b: Is a clot likely? – A normal result (<500 µg/L) essentially rules out DVT in low‑risk patients; elevated values are non‑specific.
Is there a thrombus? – Non‑compressible vein confirms DVT; if unavailable, rely on clinical probability and D‑dimer.
Is pulmonary embolism present? – May show Westermark sign or oligemia; normal film does not exclude PE.

b: LMWH: predictable effect, no routine monitoring.
Unfractionated heparin: reversible, useful if surgery may be needed soon.
Avoid warfarin monotherapy until after initial heparin because of delayed onset.
sections.p: Start anticoagulation promptly unless contraindicated. In low‑resource settings, low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred; if unavailable, unfractionated heparin infusion can be used with activated partial thromboplastin time monitoring.

b: Cellulitis: erythema, warmth, systemic fever; usually no calf swelling asymmetry.
Baker's cyst: popliteal fossa mass that enlarges with knee extension.
sections.p: Cellulitis, muscle strain, Baker's cyst, and chronic venous insufficiency can mimic DVT.

b: In HIV/TB patients, chronic inflammation elevates D‑dimer.
Obesity can make leg circumference measurements unreliable.
sections.p: D‑dimer may be raised in infection, pregnancy, or recent surgery, leading to false‑positive suspicion. Normal D‑dimer in high‑risk patients does not fully exclude proximal DVT.

b: Use Wells score to stratify risk; treat high‑risk patients empirically.
If ultrasound unavailable, repeat clinical exam after 48 h if suspicion persists.
sections.p: Focus on risk assessment, bedside signs, and the decision algorithm when imaging is not available.

b: Starting anticoagulation without assessing bleeding risk.
sections.p: Misinterpreting mild leg swelling as benign, delaying anticoagulation, or using aspirin alone for treatment.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden dyspnoea, chest pain, or syncope (possible pulmonary embolism).
Rapidly expanding leg swelling with pain (possible compartment syndrome).
